introduction-why-internals-matter-for-op.core: Long-running daemons and platforms expose Python's internals: the GIL limits CPU parallelism, context managers guarantee cleanup, decorators add cross-cutting behaviour, metaclasses build frameworks and type hints catch bugs early.

first_principles.problem: A script that 'works' becomes a daemon that leaks file descriptors, doesn't scale across cores and breaks on refactors.
truths: The runtime has specific concurrency rules.
derivation: Understand the **GIL** before choosing threads or processes.

analogy.title: Driving vs. knowing your car
analogy.story: Anyone can drive to the shop; a long-haul trucker needs to know engine limits, fuel and maintenance.
analogy.breaks: You don't need internals for quick scripts, only for long-lived or scaled code.

check.q: Why do internals matter more for daemons than scripts?
check.a: Long-lived processes expose leaks, concurrency limits and maintenance problems that short scripts never hit.

the-gil-global-interpreter-lock.core: CPython's GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time. Threads help with I/O-bound work (the GIL is released while waiting) but not with CPU-bound work, which needs multiprocessing.

first_principles.problem: Adding threads to a CPU-heavy log parser doesn't make it faster, and can make it slower.
truths: The GIL protects CPython's internal memory management.
Separate processes each have their own GIL.
derivation: Python 3.13+ offers an experimental free-threaded build.

analogy.title: Many chefs, one knife
analogy.story: Hiring more chefs doesn't speed up chopping if there's only one knife. Chefs waiting for the oven don't need the knife, though.
analogy.breaks: Native extensions like numpy release the GIL, so some CPU work does run in parallel.

example.title: Two workloads

steps.label: Result
steps.detail: Each workload uses the right concurrency model.

code.text:
# I/O: 100 HTTP calls → ThreadPoolExecutor: fast
# CPU: hash 1M files → ProcessPoolExecutor: uses all cores
with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex:
    ex.map(sha256_file, paths)

example.outcome: concurrency choices that actually speed things up.

check.q: Why do threads still help for HTTP calls?
check.a: The GIL is released while waiting on network I/O, so other threads can run.

context-managers-the-with-statement.core: A context manager pairs setup with guaranteed teardown. `with` calls `__enter__` and then `__exit__`, even if an exception occurs, so files, locks and connections are always released.

first_principles.problem: An exception between open() and close() leaks a file descriptor, and in a daemon these accumulate until it crashes.
truths: Exceptions skip any code after them.
derivation: Write your own with **@contextmanager** (yield between setup and teardown).

analogy.title: A hotel key card
analogy.story: The card activates at check-in and deactivates at check-out, however you leave.
analogy.breaks: Context managers only clean up what they manage. Resources acquired outside them are on you.

steps.label: Guarantee
steps.detail: The host is re-enabled even if the upgrade fails.

check.q: Why put teardown in `finally` inside a @contextmanager?
check.a: So it runs even when the body raises an exception.

decorators-wrapping-behavior.core: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapped version, adding behaviour such as retries, timing, logging or auth without changing the original code.

first_principles.problem: Retry and timing logic copied into 30 functions drifts and clutters the business logic.
truths: Functions are objects you can pass and return.
derivation: Write **def deco(fn): def wrapper(*a, **kw): ... return wrapper**.

analogy.title: A phone case
analogy.story: The phone works the same, but the case adds protection and a kickstand without opening the phone.
analogy.breaks: Stacking many decorators makes tracebacks and behaviour harder to follow.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One definition gives every function consistent retries.

check.a: To keep the original function's name, docstring and signature on the wrapper.

metaclasses-the-framework-builder.core: Classes are objects too, and their type is a metaclass (by default `type`). A custom metaclass runs code when a class is defined, so frameworks use them for registration, validation and auto-wiring.

first_principles.problem: A plugin system needs every subclass registered and validated automatically, without users remembering to do it.
truths: Frameworks need hooks at definition time.
derivation: Prefer the simpler **__init_subclass__** when you can.

analogy.title: A factory that builds factories
analogy.story: A metaclass is the machine that makes the moulds (classes) that make the products (instances).
analogy.breaks: Metaclasses are rarely needed in application code. Decorators or __init_subclass__ usually suffice.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: New checks register themselves just by being defined.

type-hinting-and-static-analysis-with-my.core: Type hints declare what functions expect and return, and mypy checks them without running the code. At scale they catch the None-vs-str and wrong-argument bugs before production.

first_principles.problem: Dynamic typing hides bugs until a rare runtime path receives None instead of a string.
truths: Static analysis can check them anyway.
derivation: Annotate **functions**: `def f(host: str, port: int = 22) -> bool`.
Use **Optional, list[str], dict[str, int]**, TypedDict and Protocol.

analogy.title: Labels on electrical sockets
analogy.story: You can still plug the wrong voltage in, but a checker reads the labels and warns you before you switch on.
analogy.breaks: Hints don't enforce anything at runtime. Use pydantic for validating input.

example.title: Catching a None bug

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Handle the None case before connecting.

code.text:
def get_ip(host: str) -> str | None: ...
ip = get_ip("web1")
connect(ip)  # mypy: Argument 1 has incompatible type "str | None"; expected "str"

example.outcome: a whole class of runtime crashes caught in CI.

check.q: Do type hints affect runtime behaviour?
check.a: No. They are checked statically by tools like mypy.
